# Curriculum vitae: Dr Elisavra Vardessolvi

Updated 30 September 2026.

## Personal and professional details

Elisavra Vardessolvi is an Italian citizen and a postdoctoral researcher in materials chemistry at the Università di Rocca Selvaronda, Italy. Her research concerns sulfide solid electrolytes, composite positive electrodes and the interpretation of resistance growth in laboratory solid-state cells. Her current institutional affiliation, employment and principal residence are all in Italy.

She works in the Solid-State Electrochemistry Laboratory led by Professor Martelvia Bellorvessi. Her responsibilities include preparation of lithium argyrodite electrolytes, assembly of pressure-controlled cells, electrochemical measurements and maintenance of the laboratory's analysis scripts. She is responsible for the traceability of the SULVERNEX project dataset, including sample identifiers, processing records and links between raw measurements and figures.

## Education and employment

- **1 October 2023–present:** postdoctoral researcher, Department of Chemical Materials, Università di Rocca Selvaronda, Italy. Research employment has been continuous and full time. Her current fixed-term contract runs through 30 September 2027.
- **20 July 2023:** PhD in Materials Chemistry awarded by the Università di Rocca Selvaronda. Doctoral enrolment began on 1 November 2019. Thesis: *Transport and contact evolution in pressed lithium argyrodite electrolytes*. Supervisor: Professor Martelvia Bellorvessi.
- **September 2017–July 2019:** master's degree in chemistry, Università di Rocca Selvaronda. Dissertation on impedance measurements in moisture-sensitive inorganic conductors.
- **September 2014–July 2017:** bachelor's degree in chemistry, Università di Rocca Selvaronda.

Between the doctorate and the start of her postdoctoral contract, Vardessolvi completed corrections to an accepted manuscript and deposited her thesis. She held no research appointment during that interval. There have been no parental, medical or other extended career interruptions during her postdoctoral employment.

## Research responsibilities

During her doctorate, Vardessolvi established a reproducible workflow for preparing Li6PS5Cl pellets and separating instrument, geometry and sample contributions to conductivity variation. She performed synthesis, pellet preparation and impedance measurements, and wrote the scripts used for fitting and uncertainty summaries. The thesis included laboratory powder diffraction and ex situ surface analysis conducted with specialist support.

In SULVERNEX, she designed the batch allocation and cell-testing sequence with Bellorvessi, prepared the electrolyte batches, assembled the cells and performed the electrochemical analysis. Bellorvessi was the grant holder and retained responsibility for expenditure and personnel decisions. Vardessolvi coordinated sample scheduling and the technical completion report but has not held an independent research grant or managed an institutional research budget. Since the award closed in March 2026, her duties have included dataset stewardship, manuscript preparation and maintenance of the laboratory's electrochemical analysis workflow. Her continuing appointment is supported by the department outside the closed award.

Her quantitative work uses Python, pandas, NumPy and SciPy, with version-controlled scripts and machine-readable sample manifests. She has implemented equivalent-circuit fitting, residual inspection and resampling at synthesis-batch level. She distinguishes repeated measurements of one specimen from independently prepared material. She has used exploratory distribution-of-relaxation-times analysis, but has not treated its peaks as uniquely identified chemical processes.

## Methods and training

Vardessolvi independently operates inert-atmosphere synthesis and cell-assembly workflows, potentiostats, galvanostatic cycling equipment and the laboratory powder diffractometer after local training. She has experience with air-free sample transfer, sulfide waste handling and the laboratory's hydrogen sulfide response procedures. Electron microscopy and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy measurements have been performed by facility specialists; she prepared samples and contributed to interpretation.

Her synchrotron experience consists of assisting with an ex situ diffraction experiment and reducing a supervised subset of those data. She has not independently designed or led an operando synchrotron experiment, developed an X-ray-compatible electrochemical cell or carried out X-ray absorption spectroscopy analysis. She has no experience with tomography reconstruction.

## Teaching, supervision and service

Vardessolvi has no teaching experience and no formal or informal student-supervision experience. She has not delivered a course, assessed student work, supervised a dissertation or acted as a doctoral co-supervisor. Laboratory handover records concern equipment operation among employed colleagues and do not represent student supervision.

She maintains the laboratory's sample-label conventions and has contributed to internal reproducibility discussions. She has delivered research presentations at departmental seminars. She has no experience organising a scientific conference or leading a multi-institutional project.

## Research outputs and languages

Her publication record comprises three published journal articles and one first-author manuscript under review. Two of the published articles are first-author papers. The under-review manuscript has a public preprint and has not been accepted. Full bibliographic records and contribution statements appear in the publications register.

Italian is her first language. She uses English for research writing and scientific meetings. She has no working proficiency in Swedish or French.

# SULVERNEX: final scientific report

**Batch-controlled measurements of resistance growth at sulfide composite cathode interfaces**

Project period: 1 October 2023–31 March 2026. Report approved on 30 April 2026; publication and archive status updated on 30 September 2026. Principal investigator: Professor Martelvia Bellorvessi, Università di Rocca Selvaronda. Experimental lead and report author: Dr Elisavra Vardessolvi.

## Funding and purpose

SULVERNEX received EUR 84,000 from the university's Materials Research Seed Fund, award URS-MAT-2023-017. Recorded expenditure was EUR 52,000 for research personnel, EUR 18,000 for consumables, EUR 10,000 for instrument access and EUR 4,000 for travel. These categories total EUR 84,000. Existing laboratory equipment and permanent staff time were institutional contributions outside this award.

The project examined whether a lithium niobate surface treatment of a nickel-rich layered oxide cathode was associated with lower resistance growth when the cathode was combined with Li6PS5Cl. The immediate objective was a controlled comparison under fixed laboratory conditions. Establishing the chemical sequence of interphase formation was outside the measurements available to the project.

## Materials and experimental design

Six independently synthesised Li6PS5Cl batches were prepared by the same mechanochemical and thermal protocol. Each batch supplied three conductivity pellets and four cycling cells. The conductivity dataset therefore contains 18 pellets. The cycling dataset contains 24 cells, with two coated-cathode and two uncoated-cathode cells from each electrolyte batch: 12 cells per condition.

The cathode active material was LiNi0.8Mn0.1Co0.1O2. A single parent powder lot was divided between the lithium niobate treatment and the uncoated control. The control underwent the same solvent exposure and thermal history without the niobium precursor. The comparison therefore controls those processing steps, although the coating preparation itself was not independently repeated across multiple cathode lots.

Cell assembly order was randomised within each electrolyte batch, and testing channels were balanced across conditions. Sample labels concealed condition during the first impedance-fitting pass. There was no preselection of cells on the basis of initial discharge capacity. All assembled cycling cells completed the specified cycling sequence and were included in the endpoint summaries.

Cells used lithium–indium negative electrodes and pressed sulfide separators. Cathode active-material loading was 2.0 ± 0.2 mg cm−2, and separator thickness was 500 ± 40 µm; these are means ± sample standard deviations across the 24 cells. Cycling was conducted at 25 °C under a nominal stack pressure of 10 MPa, between cell voltages of 2.2 and 3.6 V. After formation, the specific current was 18 mA g−1 of cathode active material, equivalent to C/10 using a reference capacity of 180 mAh g−1.

## Conductivity and capacity results

Room-temperature ionic conductivity was 3.1 ± 0.4 mS cm−1 at 25 °C. This is the mean ± sample standard deviation of the six batch means, each calculated from three pellets. Conductivity was calculated from pellet geometry and the fitted high-frequency electrolyte resistance using blocking electrodes. The 18 pellets were not treated as 18 independent synthesis replicates.

At cycle 5, discharge capacity was 154 ± 9 mAh g−1 for coated cathodes and 157 ± 10 mAh g−1 for uncoated cathodes. These descriptive statistics are means ± sample standard deviations across 12 cells per condition. Capacity was normalised to the mass of layered oxide, excluding the coating, electrolyte and conductive additive.

Capacity retention at cycle 100, relative to each cell's cycle-5 capacity, was 84.6 ± 4.3% for coated cathodes and 69.8 ± 6.1% for uncoated cathodes. The difference between condition means was 14.8 percentage points, with a batch-resampled 95% confidence interval of 9.6–20.0 percentage points. The standard deviations describe cell-to-cell variation; the confidence interval accounts for the shared electrolyte batch by resampling complete batch groups. It does not capture variation between cathode powder lots or coating-production runs.

## Resistance measurements

Impedance spectra were collected after cycles 5 and 100 at the same discharged endpoint, following a standard rest. The reported area-specific resistance is the fitted non-ohmic cell contribution after subtraction of the high-frequency electrolyte intercept. It is not a direct measurement of a chemically isolated cathode interphase.

For coated cathodes, area-specific resistance increased from 38 ± 7 Ω cm² at cycle 5 to 92 ± 18 Ω cm² at cycle 100. For uncoated cathodes, it increased from 41 ± 8 Ω cm² to 176 ± 31 Ω cm². Each value is a mean ± sample standard deviation across 12 cells. The corresponding mean increases were 54 Ω cm² and 135 Ω cm². Their difference was 81 Ω cm², with a batch-resampled 95% confidence interval of 58–104 Ω cm².

The coated condition therefore showed 60.0% less mean resistance growth under this protocol, calculated as (135 − 54)/135. This relative reduction concerns growth between the two measured endpoints, not a reduction in final resistance or a directly measured reduction in interphase thickness.

Equivalent-circuit fits used the same circuit family across conditions. The archive includes fitted parameters, residuals and alternative fits for spectra with overlapping features. Several circuit parameters were correlated. The fitted resistance contrast was more stable than the individual capacitance and dispersion terms, which were not assigned to specific reaction products.

## Structural observations and interpretation

Laboratory diffraction confirmed the dominant argyrodite phase before cell assembly. Ex situ synchrotron diffraction on selected recovered specimens provided checks for crystalline secondary phases. It did not resolve the amorphous interphase or establish when any decomposition product formed during cycling. Surface spectra were consistent with altered sulfur-containing environments after cycling, but air-free transfer and reference selection remained sources of uncertainty.

The electrochemical results support an association between cathode surface treatment and improved retention under the tested conditions. They do not establish whether chemical passivation, mechanical contact preservation or another treatment-related change dominated. Contributions from the lithium–indium electrode and composite contact network could not be uniquely separated from the measured non-ohmic resistance.

## Limitations and archived outputs

The study used one cathode powder lot, one coating preparation and a low-loading pellet-cell geometry. It did not test practical thin separators, pouch cells, lithium-metal compatibility or performance under low stack pressure. No cell-level energy-density estimate was produced. Conductivity at one temperature does not establish an activation energy or low-temperature performance.

The deposited dataset contains raw files for all 24 cycling cells and all 18 conductivity pellets, preparation logs, sample manifests, fitting scripts and the analysis environment specification. Data and metadata are released under CC BY 4.0; analysis code is released under the MIT licence. The institutional archive performs checksums and retains the raw vendor files alongside open-format exports. No patent application was filed for these results.

The main comparative manuscript remained under review on 30 September 2026. Its reported numerical results match this final report. The project award has closed, and its expenditure cannot be treated as an available balance.

# Publication and research-output register

Dr Elisavra Vardessolvi, Università di Rocca Selvaronda. Status checked against the author's correspondence and institutional repository on 30 September 2026.

The register contains three published journal articles and one manuscript under review. The DOI attached to the under-review item identifies its deposited preprint; it is not evidence of journal publication or acceptance. Author order below is the order on each article or manuscript. No item has been withdrawn or retracted.

## Published journal articles

### 1. Pellet geometry and contact contributions in impedance measurements of lithium argyrodites

Nestravelli, D.; Vardessolvi, E.; Bellorvessi, M. (2021). *Selvaronda Journal of Inorganic Ion Transport*, 8, 117–129.

DOI: 10.99999/pb.battery-postdoc.2021.1

Status: published, 18 November 2021. Vardessolvi is second author. She prepared pellets, measured their dimensions and collected part of the impedance dataset during her doctorate. Nestravelli led the measurement comparison and manuscript drafting. Bellorvessi supervised the research. The article addresses measurement practice and does not report the later SULVERNEX cycling experiment.

### 2. Batch variability in mechanochemically prepared Li6PS5Cl solid electrolytes

Vardessolvi, E.; Nestravelli, D.; Bellorvessi, M. (2023). *Velnarion Materials Chemistry and Ionic Transport*, 12, 204–218.

DOI: 10.99999/pb.battery-postdoc.2023.1

Status: published, 7 September 2023. Vardessolvi is first author. She developed the sample-tracking scheme, performed synthesis and conductivity measurements, analysed the data and wrote the initial manuscript. This paper derives from her doctoral work. Its batches are separate from those prepared for SULVERNEX, and its measurements must not be pooled with the final project's dataset without accounting for the changed processing records.

### 3. Reproducible resistance extraction from pressure-controlled sulfide composite cells

Vardessolvi, E.; Bellorvessi, M.; Sörnelqvist, L. (2024). *Sörvaskel Electrochemical Measurement Methods*, 6, 51–66.

DOI: 10.99999/pb.battery-postdoc.2024.1

Status: published, 12 December 2024. Vardessolvi is first author. She performed the electrochemical measurements, implemented the fitting workflow and drafted the manuscript. Bellorvessi supervised the experimental work. Sörnelqvist advised on reproducibility and the interpretation of overlapping impedance features through remote collaboration. The article reports a measurement-validation dataset rather than the complete coating comparison. Its cells are not included in the 24-cell SULVERNEX endpoint analysis.

## Manuscript under review

### 4. Cathode surface treatment moderates resistance growth in Li6PS5Cl composite cells

Vardessolvi, E.; Nestravelli, D.; Sörnelqvist, L.; Bellorvessi, M. (2026). Submitted to *Arvenquell Electrochemical Interfaces*; preprint deposited in the Selvaronda Research Archive.

DOI: 10.99999/pb.battery-postdoc.2026.1

Status: under review; submitted on 16 June 2026. Preprint deposited on 18 June 2026. No acceptance decision had been received by 30 September 2026. Vardessolvi is first author. She designed the batch allocation with Bellorvessi, performed the principal experiments, completed the statistical analysis and wrote the initial manuscript. Nestravelli contributed cathode preparation and sample-characterisation records. Sörnelqvist contributed interpretation of the structural evidence and revisions. Bellorvessi provided supervision and project administration.

This is the manuscript containing the SULVERNEX retention and resistance-growth results. Its public availability permits scrutiny of those results, but it remains an unaccepted manuscript. The repository record explicitly labels the deposited version as a preprint.

## Associated outputs and attribution

The SULVERNEX dataset and analysis code are linked from the fourth item's repository record. They are supporting research outputs and are not additional journal articles. The doctoral thesis is also deposited in the institutional archive and is not counted as a separate paper here.

There are no accepted-but-unpublished papers, patents, registered software products or additional submitted manuscripts in this register. No citation counts or journal-level metrics have been compiled. Contributor statements distinguish Vardessolvi's experimental and analytical responsibilities from grant ownership, specialist instrument operation and supervision.

# Laboratory resources and collaboration record

Record date: 30 September 2026. Prepared from laboratory inventories, access records and correspondence retained by Dr Elisavra Vardessolvi.

## Current laboratory in Italy

The Solid-State Electrochemistry Laboratory at the Università di Rocca Selvaronda is led by Professor Martelvia Bellorvessi. Dr Davrenio Nestravelli contributes inorganic synthesis and cathode-processing expertise. Vardessolvi is the postdoctoral researcher responsible for the SULVERNEX electrochemical dataset. Technical staff support instrument maintenance and waste handling through the department; they are not staff employed on an ongoing SULVERNEX award.

Existing equipment includes argon gloveboxes, a planetary mill, sealed reaction vessels, programmable furnaces, a hydraulic pellet press, pressure-monitored cell fixtures, potentiostats with impedance capability and multichannel battery cyclers. The laboratory has access to departmental powder diffraction and air-free transfer equipment. Surface spectroscopy and electron microscopy are shared services operated by specialist staff and require bookings.

These facilities support synthesis and laboratory electrochemistry. The laboratory has no synchrotron source, dedicated operando X-ray beamline or in-house X-ray absorption spectroscopy instrument. Its current cell fixtures were designed for electrochemical testing and are not certified beamline sample environments. No equipment purchase or additional staff appointment has been approved in connection with Vardessolvi's international collaborations.

## Swedish collaborating group

Dr Linnevia Sörnelqvist leads the Operando Electrochemical Structure Group at the Sörvaskel Institute of Materials Science in Uppsala, Sweden. She is a permanent group leader and an accredited doctoral supervisor. Her research concerns diffraction and total-scattering measurements during electrochemical operation, with particular attention to separating structural evolution from changes caused by sample environment and data reduction.

The group currently comprises six people: Sörnelqvist, two postdoctoral researchers, two doctoral researchers and one instrument engineer. The engineer maintains the laboratory's electrochemical sample environments and helps prepare beamline-compatible hardware. The postdoctoral researchers contribute diffraction analysis and electrochemical measurements. The doctoral researchers work on ongoing group projects and are not personnel assigned to Vardessolvi.

Existing local resources include an argon glovebox, a laboratory diffractometer equipped for electrochemical measurements, a potentiostat, pressure-controlled X-ray-compatible cell holders and a computing server for diffraction reduction and modelling. These are operating resources, not ordered equipment. Synchrotron access is obtained through external facilities; the institute does not control an independently allocated block of beamtime for Vardessolvi.

Sörnelqvist and Vardessolvi have collaborated since February 2024. Sörnelqvist is a co-author on the published methods paper and the manuscript under review, and has acted as an external scientific adviser. During Vardessolvi's June 2025 visit, the group demonstrated operando cell alignment and reviewed her resistance-fitting workflow. Vardessolvi observed the alignment procedure but did not conduct a complete operando experiment or acquire independent operator status.

Vardessolvi has no Swedish employment contract, salary, visiting appointment or student-supervision responsibility. Sörnelqvist has not been her formal doctoral or postdoctoral supervisor. The collaboration record establishes scientific contact and knowledge of the group's facilities; it does not constitute an employment appointment or a reservation of instrument time.

## Swiss synchrotron contact

Dr Lukevan Arvenstald is a beamline scientist at the Aare Veltrass Photon Facility near Villigen, Switzerland. The facility provides synchrotron diffraction and total-scattering capabilities, including staff-supported electrochemical sample environments. Arvenstald was Vardessolvi's local scientific contact during the November 2025 visit.

Vardessolvi joined an experiment led by Bellorvessi under an allocation held by the Italian laboratory. She prepared air-free samples, assisted with mounting and reduced a supervised subset of ex situ diffraction data. Arvenstald operated the beamline and checked the reduction workflow. Vardessolvi was neither the allocation's principal investigator nor an independently authorised beamline operator.

The resulting measurements informed the limited structural checks described in the SULVERNEX report. The visit did not include time-resolved cycling measurements. Arvenstald remains an established technical contact, but there is no active beamtime allocation, employment offer or formal visiting appointment held by Vardessolvi at the Swiss facility.

## Canadian collaboration offer

Dr Mirelvane Davenorrel is a staff scientist in electrochemical X-ray methods at the Prairie Velnor Light Facility in Saskatoon, Canada. Her work combines operando diffraction with practical development of air-sensitive electrochemical sample environments. The facility has existing diffraction beamlines and staff-supported preparation space for air-sensitive samples.

Davenorrel and Vardessolvi held a remote technical meeting on 6 May 2026. In a signed letter dated 22 May 2026, Davenorrel offered scientific collaboration on sulfide-cell measurements, including methodological guidance and joint interpretation of diffraction data. The letter identifies Davenorrel as the scientific contact and confirms the facility's relevant operating capabilities.

The letter is a scientific collaboration offer. It does not award beamtime, provide salary support, create a visiting appointment or bind the facility to supply staff effort for a specified period. Vardessolvi has not submitted a beamtime application there, has never visited Canada and has not worked with Davenorrel on a completed experiment or publication. Their contact is therefore less developed than the Italian–Swedish collaboration or the completed Swiss visit.

## Access and research records

Each external facility retains its own safety review, training and access procedures. Existing personal contacts do not waive those procedures. Vardessolvi's institutional account provides access to her deposited data and analysis code, but not to collaborators' unpublished datasets. No collaborator has transferred ownership of equipment, intellectual property or an unspent research allocation to her.

# Residence and research-activity record

**Elisavra Vardessolvi — statement current to 30 September 2026**

This record reconciles residence, employment and travel information held in the university personnel file and the applicant's travel records. It covers physical presence as well as institutional affiliation. Remote scientific discussions are recorded separately from travel.

Vardessolvi is an Italian citizen and has maintained her principal residence in Italy throughout her education and research career. Her bachelor's degree, master's degree, doctorate and current postdoctoral employment were all undertaken at the Università di Rocca Selvaronda. She has never held employment or enrolled in a degree programme in Sweden, Switzerland or Canada.

## Physical presence from 1 October 2023 to 30 September 2026

During this 36-month interval, Vardessolvi was physically present in Italy except for the following two research visits:

| Country | Inclusive dates | Days of physical presence | Activity |
|---|---|---:|---|
| Sweden | 10–23 June 2025 | 14 | Scientific visit to Sörnelqvist's group in Uppsala; laboratory demonstrations and analysis discussions |
| Switzerland | 3–9 November 2025 | 7 | Participation in Bellorvessi's ex situ diffraction experiment at the Aare Veltrass Photon Facility |

Arrival and departure days are included in these counts. There were no additional foreign holidays, secondments, conferences, remote-working stays or research visits during the stated interval. Physical presence in Canada was 0 days.

The two visits were the only stays in Sweden or Switzerland in Vardessolvi's life through the record date. She has never entered Canada. Neither visit involved local employment, degree enrolment or a change of principal residence. Her Italian postdoctoral employment continued during both visits.

## Collaboration and documentary basis

Meetings with Sörnelqvist outside the recorded Swedish visit took place remotely while Vardessolvi was in Italy. All contact with Davenorrel has been remote. The existence of a Swedish co-author, a Swiss beamline contact or a Canadian collaboration letter does not indicate residence in those countries.

Supporting documents comprise the Italian employment certificate, travel authorisations, transport receipts and host attendance confirmations. This statement records completed activity through 30 September 2026; it makes no assertion about subsequent travel or residence.

# INTERSUL: final scientific report

**Batch-controlled measurements of resistance growth at sulfide composite cathode interfaces**

Project period: 1 October 2023–31 March 2026. Report approved on 30 April 2026. Principal investigator: Professor Marta Bellorni, Università di Rocca Selvara. Experimental lead and report author: Dr Elisa Vardelli.

## Funding and purpose

INTERSUL received EUR 84,000 from the university's Materials Research Seed Fund, award URS-MAT-2023-017. Recorded expenditure was EUR 52,000 for research personnel, EUR 18,000 for consumables, EUR 10,000 for instrument access and EUR 4,000 for travel. These categories total EUR 84,000. Existing laboratory equipment and permanent staff time were institutional contributions outside this award.

The project examined whether a lithium niobate surface treatment of a nickel-rich layered oxide cathode was associated with lower resistance growth when the cathode was combined with Li6PS5Cl. The immediate objective was a controlled comparison under fixed laboratory conditions. Establishing the chemical sequence of interphase formation was outside the measurements available to the project.

## Materials and experimental design

Six independently synthesised Li6PS5Cl batches were prepared by the same mechanochemical and thermal protocol. Each batch supplied three conductivity pellets and four cycling cells. The conductivity dataset therefore contains 18 pellets. The cycling dataset contains 24 cells, with two coated-cathode and two uncoated-cathode cells from each electrolyte batch: 12 cells per condition.

The cathode active material was LiNi0.8Mn0.1Co0.1O2. A single parent powder lot was divided between the lithium niobate treatment and the uncoated control. The control underwent the same solvent exposure and thermal history without the niobium precursor. The comparison therefore controls those processing steps, although the coating preparation itself was not independently repeated across multiple cathode lots.

Cell assembly order was randomised within each electrolyte batch, and testing channels were balanced across conditions. Sample labels concealed condition during the first impedance-fitting pass. There was no preselection of cells on the basis of initial discharge capacity. All assembled cycling cells completed the specified cycling sequence and were included in the endpoint summaries.

Cells used lithium–indium negative electrodes and pressed sulfide separators. Cathode active-material loading was 2.0 ± 0.2 mg cm−2, and separator thickness was 500 ± 40 µm; these are means ± sample standard deviations across the 24 cells. Cycling was conducted at 25 °C under a nominal stack pressure of 10 MPa, between cell voltages of 2.2 and 3.6 V. After formation, the specific current was 18 mA g−1 of cathode active material, equivalent to C/10 using a reference capacity of 180 mAh g−1.

## Conductivity and capacity results

Room-temperature ionic conductivity was 3.1 ± 0.4 mS cm−1 at 25 °C. This is the mean ± sample standard deviation of the six batch means, each calculated from three pellets. Conductivity was calculated from pellet geometry and the fitted high-frequency electrolyte resistance using blocking electrodes. The 18 pellets were not treated as 18 independent synthesis replicates.

At cycle 5, discharge capacity was 154 ± 9 mAh g−1 for coated cathodes and 157 ± 10 mAh g−1 for uncoated cathodes. These descriptive statistics are means ± sample standard deviations across 12 cells per condition. Capacity was normalised to the mass of layered oxide, excluding the coating, electrolyte and conductive additive.

Capacity retention at cycle 100, relative to each cell's cycle-5 capacity, was 84.6 ± 4.3% for coated cathodes and 69.8 ± 6.1% for uncoated cathodes. The difference between condition means was 14.8 percentage points, with a batch-resampled 95% confidence interval of 9.6–20.0 percentage points. The standard deviations describe cell-to-cell variation; the confidence interval accounts for the shared electrolyte batch by resampling complete batch groups. It does not capture variation between cathode powder lots or coating-production runs.

## Resistance measurements

Impedance spectra were collected after cycles 5 and 100 at the same discharged endpoint, following a standard rest. The reported area-specific resistance is the fitted non-ohmic cell contribution after subtraction of the high-frequency electrolyte intercept. It is not a direct measurement of a chemically isolated cathode interphase.

For coated cathodes, area-specific resistance increased from 38 ± 7 Ω cm² at cycle 5 to 92 ± 18 Ω cm² at cycle 100. For uncoated cathodes, it increased from 41 ± 8 Ω cm² to 176 ± 31 Ω cm². Each value is a mean ± sample standard deviation across 12 cells. The corresponding mean increases were 54 Ω cm² and 135 Ω cm². Their difference was 81 Ω cm², with a batch-resampled 95% confidence interval of 58–104 Ω cm².

The coated condition therefore showed 60.0% less mean resistance growth under this protocol, calculated as (135 − 54)/135. This relative reduction concerns growth between the two measured endpoints, not a reduction in final resistance or a directly measured reduction in interphase thickness.

Equivalent-circuit fits used the same circuit family across conditions. The archive includes fitted parameters, residuals and alternative fits for spectra with overlapping features. Several circuit parameters were correlated. The fitted resistance contrast was more stable than the individual capacitance and dispersion terms, which were not assigned to specific reaction products.

## Structural observations and interpretation

Laboratory diffraction confirmed the dominant argyrodite phase before cell assembly. Ex situ synchrotron diffraction on selected recovered specimens provided checks for crystalline secondary phases. It did not resolve the amorphous interphase or establish when any decomposition product formed during cycling. Surface spectra were consistent with altered sulfur-containing environments after cycling, but air-free transfer and reference selection remained sources of uncertainty.

The electrochemical results support an association between cathode surface treatment and improved retention under the tested conditions. They do not establish whether chemical passivation, mechanical contact preservation or another treatment-related change dominated. Contributions from the lithium–indium electrode and composite contact network could not be uniquely separated from the measured non-ohmic resistance.

## Limitations and archived outputs

The study used one cathode powder lot, one coating preparation and a low-loading pellet-cell geometry. It did not test practical thin separators, pouch cells, lithium-metal compatibility or performance under low stack pressure. No cell-level energy-density estimate was produced. Conductivity at one temperature does not establish an activation energy or low-temperature performance.

The deposited dataset contains raw files for all 24 cycling cells and all 18 conductivity pellets, preparation logs, sample manifests, fitting scripts and the analysis environment specification. Data and metadata are released under CC BY 4.0; analysis code is released under the MIT licence. The institutional archive performs checksums and retains the raw vendor files alongside open-format exports. No patent application was filed for these results.

The main comparative manuscript remained under review on 31 August 2026. Its reported numerical results match this final report. The project award has closed, and its expenditure cannot be treated as an available balance.

# Laboratory resources and collaboration record

Record date: 31 August 2026. Prepared from laboratory inventories, access records and correspondence retained by Dr Elisa Vardelli.

## Current laboratory in Italy

The Solid-State Electrochemistry Laboratory at the Università di Rocca Selvara is led by Professor Marta Bellorni. Dr Davide Nestri contributes inorganic synthesis and cathode-processing expertise. Vardelli is the postdoctoral researcher responsible for the INTERSUL electrochemical dataset. Technical staff support instrument maintenance and waste handling through the department; they are not staff employed on an ongoing INTERSUL award.

Existing equipment includes argon gloveboxes, a planetary mill, sealed reaction vessels, programmable furnaces, a hydraulic pellet press, pressure-monitored cell fixtures, potentiostats with impedance capability and multichannel battery cyclers. The laboratory has access to departmental powder diffraction and air-free transfer equipment. Surface spectroscopy and electron microscopy are shared services operated by specialist staff and require bookings.

These facilities support synthesis and laboratory electrochemistry. The laboratory has no synchrotron source, dedicated operando X-ray beamline or in-house X-ray absorption spectroscopy instrument. Its current cell fixtures were designed for electrochemical testing and are not certified beamline sample environments. No equipment purchase or additional staff appointment has been approved in connection with Vardelli's international collaborations.

## Swedish collaborating group

Dr Linnea Sörnevik leads the Operando Electrochemical Structure Group at the Sörviken Institute of Materials Science in Uppsala, Sweden. She is a permanent group leader and an accredited doctoral supervisor. Her research concerns diffraction and total-scattering measurements during electrochemical operation, with particular attention to separating structural evolution from changes caused by sample environment and data reduction.

The group currently comprises six people: Sörnevik, two postdoctoral researchers, two doctoral researchers and one instrument engineer. The engineer maintains the laboratory's electrochemical sample environments and helps prepare beamline-compatible hardware. The postdoctoral researchers contribute diffraction analysis and electrochemical measurements. The doctoral researchers work on ongoing group projects and are not personnel assigned to Vardelli.

Existing local resources include an argon glovebox, a laboratory diffractometer equipped for electrochemical measurements, a potentiostat, pressure-controlled X-ray-compatible cell holders and a computing server for diffraction reduction and modelling. These are operating resources, not ordered equipment. Synchrotron access is obtained through external facilities; the institute does not control an independently allocated block of beamtime for Vardelli.

Sörnevik and Vardelli have collaborated since February 2024. Sörnevik is a co-author on the published methods paper and the manuscript under review, and has acted as an external scientific adviser. During Vardelli's June 2025 visit, the group demonstrated operando cell alignment and reviewed her resistance-fitting workflow. Vardelli observed the alignment procedure but did not conduct a complete operando experiment or acquire independent operator status.

Vardelli has no Swedish employment contract, salary, visiting appointment or student-supervision responsibility. Sörnevik has not been her formal doctoral or postdoctoral supervisor. The collaboration record establishes scientific contact and knowledge of the group's facilities; it does not constitute an employment appointment or a reservation of instrument time.
